The '''Brahmaputra''' ({{ipa|as|ˈbɹɔɦ.mɔ.put.ɹɔ|lang}}) is a [[trans-boundary river]] which flows through [[Southwestern China]], [[Northeastern India]], and [[Bangladesh]]. It is known as the Brahmaputra in Assam, [[Yarlung Tsangpo]] in [[Lhasa Tibetan|Tibetan]], the Siang/Dihang River in the [[Miju languages|Mishmi language]], and [[Jamuna River (Bangladesh)|Jamuna River]] in [[Bangladesh]]. By itself, it is the 9th [[List of rivers by discharge|largest river]] in the world by discharge, and the 15th [[List of rivers by length|longest]].

It originates in the [[Manasarovar Lake]] region, near [[Mount Kailash]], on the northern side of the [[Himalayas]] in [[Burang County]] of [[Tibet Autonomous Region|Tibet]] where it is known as the [[Yarlung Tsangpo River]].<ref name="xinhua" /> The Brahmaputra flows along southern Tibet to break through the Himalayas in great gorges (including the [[Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon]]) and into Arunachal Pradesh.<ref name="britannica">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Brahmaputra-River |title=Brahmaputra River |website=[[Encyclopædia Britannica]] |access-date=13 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170130005707/https://www.britannica.com/place/Brahmaputra-River |archive-date=30 January 2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> It enters India near the village of [[Gelling, Arunachal Pradesh|Gelling]] in [[Arunachal Pradesh]] and flows southwest through the [[Assam]] Valley as the Brahmaputra and south through [[Bangladesh]] as the [[Jamuna River (Bangladesh)|Jamuna]] (not to be confused with the [[Yamuna River|Yamuna]] of India). In the vast [[Ganges Delta]], it merges with the [[Ganges]], popularly known as the [[Padma River|Padma]] in Bangladesh, and becomes the [[Meghna River|Meghna]] and ultimately empties into the [[Bay of Bengal]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Brahmaputra River Flowing Down From Himalayas Towards Bay of Bengal|url=http://www.eosnap.com/tag/brahmaputra-river/|access-date=22 November 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111106133618/http://www.eosnap.com/tag/brahmaputra-river/|archive-date=6 November 2011|url-status=live}}</ref>

At {{cvt|3,000|km|mi|abbr=on}} long, the Brahmaputra is an important river for [[irrigation]] and transportation in the region.<ref name="Flood Inundation Mapping of the Sparsely Gauged Large-Scale Brahmaputra Basin Using Remote Sensing Products"/><ref name="xinhua" /> The average depth of the river is {{convert|30|m|ft|abbr=on|-1}} and its maximum depth is {{convert|135|m|ft|abbr=on|-1}} (at [[Sadiya]]).<ref name=BBWR>{{cite book
 |last1= Singh
 |first1= Vijay
 |last2= Sharma
 |first2= Nayan
 |last3= Ojha
 |first3= C. Shekhar P.
 |date= 29 February 2004
 |title= The Brahmaputra Basin Water Resources
 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=HUXrVyUk0RAC
 |location= Dordrecht
 |publisher= Springer
 |page= 120
 |isbn= 9789048164813
 |access-date= 15 November 2015
 |archive-date= 20 August 2021
 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210820081154/https://books.google.com/books?id=HUXrVyUk0RAC
 |url-status= live
 }}</ref> The river is prone to catastrophic flooding in the spring when the Himalayan snow melts. The average discharge of the Brahmaputra is about ~{{cvt|22,000|m3/s|cuft/s|abbr=on}},<ref name="Flood Inundation Mapping of the Sparsely Gauged Large-Scale Brahmaputra Basin Using Remote Sensing Products"/><ref name="britannica"/> and floods reach about {{cvt|103,000|m3/s|cuft/s|abbr=on}}.<ref name="Flood Inundation Mapping of the Sparsely Gauged Large-Scale Brahmaputra Basin Using Remote Sensing Products"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fao.org/nr/water/aquastat/countries/bangladesh/index.stm |title=Water Resources of Bangladesh |website=FAO |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090806192531/http://www.fao.org/nr/water/aquastat/countries/bangladesh/index.stm |archive-date=6 August 2009 |access-date=18 November 2010}}</ref> It is a classic example of a [[braided river]] and is highly susceptible to [[River channel migration|channel migration]] and [[Avulsion (river)|avulsion]].<ref name="Catling1992">{{cite book |last=Catling |first=David |date=1992 |title=Rice in deep water |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N5JxwKx1RAgC&pg=PA177 |publisher=[[International Rice Research Institute]] |page=177 |isbn=978-971-22-0005-2 |access-date=15 November 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160514103756/https://books.google.com/books?id=N5JxwKx1RAgC&pg=PA177 |archive-date=14 May 2016 |url-status=live }}</ref> It is also one of the few rivers in the world that exhibits a [[tidal bore]]. It is navigable for most of its length.

The Brahmaputra drains the Himalayas east of the Indo-Nepal border, south-central portion of the Tibetan plateau above the [[Ganga]] basin, south-eastern portion of Tibet, the Patkai hills, the northern slopes of the [[Meghalaya]] hills, the Assam plains, and northern Bangladesh. The basin, especially south of Tibet, is characterized by high levels of rainfall. [[Kangchenjunga]] (8,586 m) is the highest point within the Brahmaputra basin and the only peak above 8,000 m.

The Brahmaputra's upper course was long unknown, and its identity with the Yarlung Tsangpo was only established by exploration in 1884–1886. The river is often called the Tsangpo-Brahmaputra river.{{Citation needed|date=July 2020}}

The lower reaches are sacred to [[Hinduism|Hindus]]. While most rivers on the Indian subcontinent have female names, this river has a rare male name. Brahmaputra means "son of [[Brahma]]" in [[Sanskrit]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Gopal |first=Madan |date=1990 |editor=K.S. Gautam |title=India through the ages|url=https://archive.org/details/indiathroughages00mada |publisher=Publication Division, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Government of India |page=[https://archive.org/details/indiathroughages00mada/page/80 80]}}</ref>
